bottle.name: Talisker 10 Year Old Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.class: Single malt Scotch whisky; an island malt from Skye, Highland in law
bottle.mash: Malted barley only, as the law asks of a single malt; the house describes it as smoky and publishes no peating level.
bottle.still: Distilled twice at Carbost in five copper pot stills, two wash and three spirit, a layout kept from triple distillation. The wash stills' lyne arms dip in a U-bend with a purifier that returns some spirit, and wooden worm tubs outside condense the rest.
bottle.wood: At least ten years in American oak casks, according to the producer. The bottling is sold as the 10 Year Old.
bottle.taste: Seawater, smoke and a lemony sweetness on the nose, then barley malt, dried fruit and a strong note of black pepper, with a warming, peppery finish that lasts.
bottle.pour: Neat, adding water drop by drop, or long with soda and ice in a highball, where the pepper and smoke carry.

label.means: Made only from malted barley, in pot stills, at the one distillery at Carbost.
Distilled and matured in Scotland, at least three years in oak, and bottled at 40% ABV or more.

records.table: Beside Loch Harport at Carbost, on Skye, Talisker has made whisky since 1830, and Talisker 10 Year Old carries sea spray and smoke, then dried fruit and a burst of black pepper. Offer it neat, with a little water on the side.
records.story: In 1830 two brothers who had come to Skye from the Isle of Eigg, the MacAskills, founded a distillery at Carbost, on the shore of Loch Harport, with a lease from the MacLeods. Robert Louis Stevenson (1850 to 1894) named it in 1880, in his poem The Scotsman's Return from Abroad, as one of the king of drinks beside Islay and Glenlivet. The distillery passed to the Distillers Company in 1925, and in 1928 it gave up triple distillation for double, though it kept its three spirit stills beside the two for the wash. In November 1960 a fire burned down the house where the stills stood, and the stills were rebuilt as exact copies of the old ones so that the spirit would not change; the old worm tubs outside were spared. The distillery's own maltings closed in 1972. At the end of the 1980s the 10 Year Old was chosen as one of the Classic Malts, the island malt of the set. Hand the 10 Year Old to a guest curious about maritime Scotch: salt, smoke and pepper together.

others.name: Talisker Distillers Edition
others.note: A second maturation in casks seasoned with Amoroso sherry, bottled by vintage at 45.8% ABV.

traps: Talisker is an island malt, but in law it is a Highland single malt: the Scotch Whisky Regulations protect no Islands region, only Islay and Campbeltown as localities.
Talisker is made on Skye, not on Islay: it is often poured beside Islay malts for its smoke, but its home is Carbost on Loch Harport.

cards.prompt: Why does Talisker run three spirit stills beside two wash stills?
cards.answer: The layout was kept from triple distillation, which Talisker gave up for double distillation in 1928.

cards.prompt: In which year was Talisker founded, and where?
cards.answer: In 1830, at Carbost on Loch Harport, Isle of Skye, by two brothers from the Isle of Eigg.

quiz.q: A guest on a distillery tour asks why Talisker has three spirit stills and two wash stills. What is the reason?
options: A rule of the Scotch law
A way to add peat smoke
quiz.explain: Talisker was triple distilled until 1928 and kept the stills when it moved to double distillation; the Scotch law sets no number of stills.

quiz.explain: Two brothers from Eigg founded Talisker in 1830; 1798 is the year Highland Park and Tobermory give for their own beginnings.

report: The plan's note is settled for the year: Wikipedia and Difford's give 1830 for the founding by Hugh and Kenneth MacAskill, with 1831 for the opening at Carbost after the lease, so the record gives 1830 as the founding. Both brothers are named as founders in both sources, but no two sources read gave either brother's death, so the record calls them two brothers from Eigg, the MacAskills, and names neither in full. The Ledger's islands style names them in a quiz stem; the integrator may wish to bring that in line.

Sources differ on the sale history: Master of Malt and Whisky Magazine have a blenders' consortium in 1898 or 1916 before the Distillers Company in 1925 (Wikipedia, Grace's Guide); the record keeps only 1925.
The Classic Malts year is given as 1988 by Wikipedia and 1989 by Difford's, so the record says the end of the 1980s.

Difford's tells the 1960 fire as a valve left open on a spirit still; one source only, so the cause is left out. Difford's says the worm tub coils survived the fire and the wooden tubs were replaced in 1997 and 1998; an Edinburgh page says the tubs survived, so the record says only that the old worm tubs were spared.

Left out for want of a source: the peating level, the source of the malt, the label's exact front wording (no page showed it, so the label terms are the class words alone), and Talisker Skye and Talisker Storm, which were not confirmed in detail.

bottle.name: Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour Single Malt Scotch Whisky
bottle.class: Single malt Scotch whisky; an island malt from Orkney, Highland in law
bottle.mash: Malted barley only. About a fifth is malted on the distillery's own floors and dried over peat cut on Hobbister Moor, made largely of heather; the rest is bought in already malted.
bottle.still: Distilled in copper pot stills at Kirkwall, beside the kilns where the house dries its own malt after turning it by hand on the malting floor.
bottle.wood: Twelve years, mostly in sherry seasoned casks of European and American oak, first fill among them, with refill casks rounding out the vatting, by the producer's account.
bottle.taste: Heather honey and a soft, aromatic peat smoke, with rich fruitcake, winter spices and Seville orange; the smoke stays sweet and gentle beneath the honey.
bottle.pour: Neat or cut with a little water, or over ice; a gentle first island malt for a guest who is wary of smoke.

label.means: The name the 12 Year Old took in 2017, when the core range was given Viking names; the whisky did not change.
Only malted barley, through pot stills, and all of it made at the distillery in Kirkwall.

records.table: Peat made largely of heather, cut on Orkney, dries part of the malt for Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour, made at Kirkwall: heather honey first, then orange and fruitcake, with a soft, sweet smoke that never takes the lead.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1798 and to a church beadle who, as the brand tells it, distilled on the side and hid his whisky beneath the pulpit when the excise men came. Other accounts credit a farmer who took the High Park estate above Kirkwall that year and built the distillery there, and several give 1826 as the year it first took out a licence. What sets it apart is the malt. The house turns part of its barley by hand on its own floors, about a fifth of what it needs, and dries it in its kilns over peat cut on Hobbister Moor, a few miles away. Orkney peat is made largely of heather, and its smoke is sweet and floral rather than tarry. Much of the whisky rests in dunnage warehouses with earth floors, and the house says the steady island climate takes less spirit from the casks than the mainland does. In 2017 the core range took Viking names to tell of Orkney's Norse past, and the 12 Year Old became Viking Honour, with the whisky unchanged. It proves to a doubtful guest that peat need not taste of tar: honey comes first, and the smoke second.

Viking Honour marks no cask and no finish: the 12 Year Old took the name in 2017 and its recipe stayed as it was.

records.table: Jura 12 Year Old comes from the island's whisky distillery at Craighouse, and twelve years in bourbon casks give it peach, bright citrus and toasted walnut, fruit rather than smoke. It took the place of the 10 in 2025, and it suits a glass neat or a highball.
records.story: The laird of the island founded a distillery at Craighouse in 1810, by the house's own account, at first called the Small Isles distillery, and it was licensed in 1831. Later in the century James Ferguson and Sons took it over. It closed in 1901; the roof came off, the buildings fell into ruin, and the island lost the work the distillery had given. In 1960 two landowners of the island set out to rebuild it, so that islanders would have work again, and brought in a designer to draw a new distillery on the old site. It reopened in 1963, with tall copper stills. Whyte and Mackay bought the distillery in the early 1990s, and in 2018 the range was relaunched, with a 10 Year Old finished in Oloroso sherry casks at its start. In August 2025 the house announced that a 12 Year Old would take the place of the 10 at the head of its age-stated range, citing consumer taste tests, and the 12 reached British shelves that October in a new pack before going further afield. Behind a bar it is the gentle island malt, fruit and walnut rather than smoke.

bottle.class: Single malt Scotch whisky, from the Isle of Arran
bottle.mash: Malted barley only; the Arran malt is unpeated, and the distillery's peated spirit is bottled under its own name, Machrie Moor.
bottle.still: Distilled at Lochranza, in the north of the island, in copper pot stills; spirit first ran there on 29 June 1995.
bottle.wood: Ten years, mainly in bourbon casks, with a portion finished for about nine months in first-fill Oloroso sherry casks before vatting, as the producer gives it.

records.table: Unpeated and bottled at 46% ABV with no chill filtering and no added colour, Arran 10 Year Old is the single malt of Lochranza, in the north of the Isle of Arran: citrus, honey and apple, then cinnamon and hazelnut. A little water opens the fruit.
records.story: Arran had gone without a legal distillery for more than 150 years when a former director of Chivas Brothers set out to build one at Lochranza, in the north of the island. Building began on 16 December 1994 and, by the house's account, was halted for a while so that a pair of golden eagles could nest on a cliff above the site. Spirit first ran through the stills on 29 June 1995, and the distillery was opened officially on 17 August that year. The Queen opened its visitor centre in 1997. The malt was left unpeated, and when the house began to make peated spirit it bottled it under another name, Machrie Moor. In 2019 the company opened a second distillery, at Lagg in the south of the island, and gave its single malts a new look, with the Lochranza Distillery name on the label and, as the house put it, the same whisky inside. Fresh and fruity, bottled at 46 per cent without chill filtering, the 10 Year Old is the answer to a guest who believes every island whisky is smoky.

bottle.class: Single malt Scotch whisky; an island malt from Mull, Highland in law
bottle.mash: Malted barley only, and unpeated; the distillery's heavily peated spirit is bottled under another name, Ledaig.
bottle.still: Distilled in copper pot stills at the distillery on the harbour at Tobermory, modernised during a closure from 2017 to 2019.

records.table: From the harbour town on Mull that gives it its name, Tobermory 12 Year Old is the distillery's unpeated malt, twelve years in American oak at 46.3% ABV, with orange, caramel and vanilla over clove. Ledaig, the peated malt, comes off the same stills.
records.story: A merchant of the harbour town founded a distillery on the shore at Tobermory in 1798, by the house's account, and called it Ledaig. Its story is one of long silences. It closed in 1837 and did not distil again until the 1870s. The Distillers Company took it over in 1916 and shut it around 1930, and it stayed silent for more than forty years. It reopened in 1972 under the Ledaig name and closed again in 1975; after more stops and starts, it was distilling again by 1990. The house kept the old name, Ledaig, for its heavily peated malt and Tobermory for the unpeated one. From 2017 to 2019 the distillery closed again, this time for refurbishment, and when it reopened in 2019 the 12 Year Old replaced the 10 as the unpeated malt's signature bottling, beside a new gin. Peat, the 12 and Ledaig together show, is the house's choice and not the island's.

others.note: The heavily peated malt of the same distillery and stills, at ten years.

traps: Tobermory and Ledaig come from one distillery: Tobermory is the unpeated malt, Ledaig the heavily peated one, and Ledaig was once the distillery's own name.
The 10 Year Old was replaced by the 12 when the distillery reopened in 2019; a bottle of the 10 on an older shelf is the earlier flagship, not a sister.
